title: Under the Tanks
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 19 of 40
content:
The first time Danse slept beside me, nothing happened.

That was the problem.

A radstorm grounded all flights and kept half the Prydwen awake while green lightning flashed outside the hull.

The storm put the maintenance crew on a different schedule. Every time the airship lurched, boots hurried along the corridor outside my bunk and somebody called a pressure reading down to the next deck.

Danse noticed the sound before I did.

“That one's the stabilizer check,” he said after a metal clang. “And that's someone dropping a wrench.”

“How can you tell?”

“Because the wrench is followed by profanity. The stabilizer isn't.”

I laughed despite myself. Then another gust knocked the cup off my shelf, and the laughter went out of me.

Danse bent to pick it up. He didn't tell me there was nothing to fear. That would have been an insult to both of us. We were in the air, inside a ship with working machinery and tired people watching it through a storm.

“I can ask the crew for a status report,” he said.

“You don't have to order anyone down here.”

“I wasn't going to.”

He stopped himself and gave me the smallest grimace. “I was considering it.”

We waited for the scheduled announcement. When it came, the captain reported the ship stable and all flights grounded until the radstorm passed. It was more useful than an invented reassurance.

“Can you stay?” I asked.

“For as long as you want company.”

“Even if I don't sleep?”

He took off his boots and sat on the far edge of the bunk, leaving me room to choose how close to move.

“Especially then,” he said. “I dislike the sound of your silence more than the ship.”

I rested against his shoulder. His shirt smelled faintly of clean cotton and machine oil, and for a moment we were not two people waiting to be brave. We were two frightened adults who had agreed not to leave the other guessing. The airship shifted in the wind. Every metal sound became a reminder that we were suspended over Boston by engineering and collective confidence.

I hated it.

Danse discovered this at approximately 0100 when he found me sitting fully dressed on my bunk.

“You’re awake.”

“So are you.”

“I’m on watch.”

“Convenient.”

A green flash lit the narrow quarters.

The ship creaked.

My hands tightened around the edge of the mattress.

Danse noticed.

He always noticed.

“Storm bothering you?”

“No.”

Another impact of thunder.

I flinched.

He folded his arms.

“Your lying needs work.”

“Your coffee needs work.”

“Unrelated.”

“Still true.”

Danse looked around the sleeping bay. Most of the bunks were occupied. Someone snored nearby with the confidence of a person who had accepted death.

“You want to walk?” he asked.

“Where?”

“Anywhere with fewer hydrogen tanks over your head.”

“You admitted those were hydrogen?”

“I said mostly.”

“Danse.”

He smiled.

We ended up in a maintenance alcove with two folding chairs and a view through a small reinforced port.

The storm rolled over the city below. Green radiation lit ruined towers from within the clouds.

Danse handed me Rad-X.

“I already took some.”

“Take another.”

“That sounds medically irresponsible.”

“I checked the dosage.”

Of course he had.

We sat.

The wind shook the hull.

I gripped the chair.

Danse put his hand over mine.

No speech.

No question.

Just pressure and warmth.

My fingers loosened.

“You afraid of anything?” I asked.

“Yes.”

The immediate answer surprised me.

“What?”

He looked out the port.

“Failing people who depend on me.”

“I guessed that one.”

“Losing control of a situation.”

“Also guessed.”

He hesitated.

“Being buried alive.”

I turned toward him.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Collapsed building when I was younger. Scavenging.”

“How long?”

“Several hours.”

“Alone?”

“Yes.”

I squeezed his hand.

He looked down at our fingers.

“Your turn.”

“Storms on airships, apparently.”

“That’s specific.”

“Commitment to craft.”

“What else?”

I stared at the storm.

“Depending on people.”

Danse went still.

“Why?”

“Same reason as you, probably. If you depend on someone, they can disappear.”

He understood too quickly.

The conversation did not need details.

We sat holding hands while the Prydwen shook.

At some point my head rested against his shoulder.

At some point his cheek touched the top of my head.

At some point I stopped listening for every change in the engines.

When the storm weakened, I should have gone back to my bunk.

I did not.

Danse should have returned to watch.

He did not.

The two folding chairs were terrible for sleeping. Eventually we gave up and returned to the quarters.

My bunk was narrow.

Danse looked at it.

Then at me.

“This is a bad idea.”

“Probably.”

“Regulations—”

“We’re sleeping.”

“I know.”

“Fully clothed.”

“I know.”

“You’re the one making it weird.”

“I am not making it weird.”

“Then lie down.”

He stared at me like I had ordered him to assault Maxson.

Finally he removed his boots and lay on top of the blanket beside me.

There was barely room.

His shoulder pressed against the wall. I was half against his chest.

“This is ridiculous,” he whispered.

“Shh. Some of us are trying to sleep.”

“You started this.”

“Good night, Paladin.”

A long pause.

Then his arm settled carefully around me.

Not possessive.

Protective almost by habit, except there was nothing to protect me from except the storm.

Maybe that was enough.

I could feel his heartbeat beneath my cheek.

Steady.

Human, my mind supplied automatically.

I did not know why the thought came with emphasis.

Danse’s fingers rested against my shoulder.

“Comfortable?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

Minutes passed.

His breathing slowed.

The storm moved east.

Nothing happened.

No kiss. No confession. We slept, sharing the quiet without asking the night to become anything more.

In the morning I woke to Danse already awake, staring at the ceiling with the expression of a man who had discovered a tactical error with no approved procedure.

“Morning,” I whispered.

He looked down at me.

“Morning.”

Neither of us moved.

Someone coughed from the next row of bunks.

Danse’s eyes widened.

I bit my lip.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“I’m asleep.”

He extracted himself with impossible care and put on his boots.

At the door he paused.

“For the record…”

“Yes?”

He looked profoundly uncomfortable.

“I slept well.”

My chest warmed.

“Me too.”

Danse nodded and left.

Five minutes later Haylen walked past my bunk, glanced at the empty space beside me, and smiled without saying a word.

I decided silence could be an act of violence.

The second time he slept beside me was deliberate.

That made it more frightening.

A radstorm rolled over Cambridge after midnight, turning the windows green and making the old police station groan in its frame. I was awake counting seconds between thunder when Danse appeared beside my bunk.

He wore fatigues and socks.

The socks somehow made the entire situation more intimate.

“Can’t sleep?” I asked.

“No.”

“Nightmares?”

A pause.

“Yes.”

He did not elaborate.

I moved over.

Danse looked at the space.

“You don’t have to—”

“Get in before Rhys wakes up and turns this into a military incident.”

That got him moving.

The bunk was not built for two people, especially when one of them was Danse. We arranged ourselves with the logistical seriousness of planning an assault.

“Your elbow is in my ribs.”

“Your knee is occupying most of the lower mattress.”

“I have two knees.”

“I’m aware.”

“Then be grateful only one is a problem.”

He made a quiet choking sound.

“Was that a laugh?”

“No.”

“Coward.”

Eventually we settled facing each other.

Lightning flickered through the curtains.

Danse’s face was close enough that I could see the shadow beneath his eyes.

“What happens in the dreams?” I asked.

His gaze went to the ceiling.

“Different things.”

“Useful.”

“Sometimes Gladius.”

His voice dropped.

“Sometimes Cutler.”

I waited.

“Sometimes I arrive too late. Sometimes I’m there in time and it changes nothing.”

“That sounds worse.”

“It is.”

Thunder rolled over the station.

Danse’s hand lay between us, open on the blanket.

I placed mine beside it, not touching.

He closed the distance.

“I don’t understand why the mind does that,” he said. “Reconstructs failures with new details as if repetition can produce a different result.”

“Maybe it’s trying to solve something that can’t be solved.”

“That’s inefficient.”

“The brain did not consult the Brotherhood manual.”

“Clearly.”

His thumb moved over the side of my hand.

The storm flashed again.

“You make it quieter,” he said.

I almost asked what he meant.

Then I understood.

Not the weather.

I swallowed.

“So do you.”

Danse looked back at me.

For a moment I thought he might kiss me.

He did not.

Instead he shifted closer until his forehead rested against mine.

The contact was so careful it hurt more than a kiss probably would have.

We stayed that way through another roll of thunder.

Eventually his breathing slowed.

Mine followed.

I woke before dawn with Danse asleep on his side, one hand curled loosely into my shirt as if sometime during the night he had needed proof I was still there.

I did not move until he woke on his own.

When his eyes opened, confusion lasted half a second.

Sometime before dawn the storm became rain.

The sound changed from violent impacts against the hull to a steady metallic tapping. Danse stirred but did not wake.

Without the power armor and uniform, sleep made him look younger. Less like a paladin and more like the scrap trader he had once described in fragments: a man from Rivet City who had learned to sleep lightly because possessions vanished and trouble did not announce itself.

His grip tightened once in my shirt.

I thought about waking him.

Instead I rested my hand over his.

The tension in his fingers eased.

It struck me then that Danse’s idea of safety had always involved being the person awake enough to provide it. Guard duty. Perimeter checks. Armor between danger and everyone else.

He did not know what to do with safety offered back.

Maybe this was the smallest version of it.

A storm passing.

A bunk too narrow for two people.

Someone still there when he opened his eyes.

Then memory returned.

His hand released my shirt immediately.

“Apologies.”

“No.”

He blinked.

“No apologizing for sleeping.”

“That was not—”

“Or for holding onto me.”

His face went red.

I smiled.

“Good morning.”

Danse stared at me, helpless for once.

Then he sighed.

“Good morning.”

We ate breakfast in near silence.

Danse attempted to behave as if waking with his hand twisted in my shirt had been an ordinary logistical event.

I allowed this fiction until he reached for the salt and knocked over his own cup.

He stared at the spreading coffee.

I stared at him.

“Say nothing.”

“I haven’t.”

“Your face is saying plenty.”

“Operationally?”

He closed his eyes.

I cleaned the spill before he could turn embarrassment into retreat. When I handed him the rag, our fingers touched.

This time he left them there for one extra second.

Outside, the radstorm had passed.

Inside, something else had not.
